positions.claim: Hardware engineering that currently lives in spreadsheets should be rewritten as real software with automated testing and continuous integration, because that is what collapses iteration cost.
You can change regulations by building the thing and explaining why it's safe — the objection to building in regulated industries is overstated.

Whether to engage regulators early or launch first is contextual: launch-first works when an entrenched incumbent is weaponizing the regulator, engage-first works for safety-critical products with no active opponent.
Most regulation originates not from public-safety concern but from incumbents using government to block competition, which he calls deeply unethical.
The 'why now' question misleads founders; many multi-billion-dollar ideas are technically feasible years before anyone starts them, and supersonic flight was one of them.
America cannot beat China by repatriating the manufacturing that left; it must invent the next generation of manufacturing, e.g. tooling-free digital processes for turbine blades.
Outside aerospace suppliers make fast iteration impossible, so building your own machine shop and test stands is worth the capital cost.
Boom's need for software engineers has increased as AI lowered the cost of software, because someone must keep architectures coherent when everyone can code.
The premise that experience wins in hardware is false, and deep expertise is actively harmful because expertise is steeped in the past.
Boom's prototype (XB-1) was too ambitious; a simpler prototype giving multiple shots on goal would have reached proof of concept in two to three years instead of ten.
Caring cannot be taught, so it should be the primary hiring filter — above skills, knowledge, and credentials.

Founders do not need to be in San Francisco — Boom left for Denver because physical-world manufacturing at scale is not affordable in the Bay Area — but should be in some ambitious ecosystem absent a specific reason.
Work-life balance is the wrong frame; work-life harmony is achievable, and being a parent and a CEO are synergistic rather than opposed.
Amazon's advantage came from pairing seven-year planning horizons with day-to-day operational excellence and refusing to massage quarterly results.
Self-belief is not a prerequisite for starting something audacious; it arrives late, and the right move is to redirect mental energy from 'can I' to 'how.'
